newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik rebels pledge to release hostages.
newsitem.headline: Tajik rebels pledge to release hostages.

text.p: Islamic rebels renewed a pledge to free six foreign and local hostages on Monday after face-to-face talks with Tajikistan's president.

The hostages, who include five U.N. workers, "would be freed in a few hours near the village of Qalai Nav some five km (three miles) from Obigarm", the rebels told reporters after the talks in Obigarm, 80 km (50 miles) from the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Neither the presidential side nor the rebels provided details of the agreements reached during the closed-door meeting, which followed the collapse of an earlier deal.
President Imomali Rakhmonov travelled to Obigarm with a top level government delegation on Monday for the talks to try to break a deadlock in the 14-day-old hostage crisis.
Russia, which views Tajikistan as a barrier against the spread of Islamic fundamentalism, has also played a key role in negotiations to free the hostages.

The rebels, led by Saidmurod Kiyomutdinov, arrived three hours late for the talks with Rakhmonov, bringing Tajik Security Minister Saidamir Zukhurov, who was captured during earlier negotiations, Russia's Itar-Tass news agency said.

The rebels told reporters Zukhurov had now been freed to take part in the talks to free the remaining five hostages: two U.N. observers -- a Swiss and a Ukranian -- and three representatives of the U.N. refugee agency.
It was not clear where the five other hostages were and Tajik officials were not immediately available to comment.

The crisis erupted on February 4, when a rebel group led by Bakhrom Sadirov seized the first of the hostages and demanded that the government allow Bakhrom's brother Rizvon and some 40 supporters to join him from neighbouring Afghanistan.
The Tajik authorities allowed more than 30 armed fighters to reach Sadirov's base on Saturday on the understanding that he would then free all his captives.
But only some of the hostages were released.

A Western diplomat said earlier that prospects for the remaining captives' release -- already promised after the government surrendered a group of rebel fighters and arms to the group on Friday -- were unclear.
Government officials in this Central Asian state said they had received promises from the Sadirovs that the hostages would not be harmed and would be freed after the talks with Rakhmonov.
The delegation travelling with Rakhmonov also included the country's deputy prime minister, the defence minister and his deputy, and other officials, Tass said.

"Bakhrom said he was ready to negotiate directly with the president and the president readily accepted the proposal," Rakhmonov's spokesman Zafar Saidov said on Sunday, adding that the rebel leader gave assurances the hostages would not be harmed.
"Don't worry about the hostages. Nothing threatens their lives," he quoted Bakhrom Sadirov as saying.
But the two Tajik sides have little trust in each other and it was only the intervention of Russia which led to negotiations resulting in earlier releases of some hostages.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin warned on Friday that Russia would take all necessary means to save the lives of the hostages.
A Russian-led force of about 20,000 border guards and military peacekeepers are stationed in the former Soviet republic, torn apart by a four-year civil war.
